title: The Dog and the Flask
text:
"My pretty dog, good dog, dear mutt, come here and breathe an excellent perfume, bought at the best perfumery in the city."


And the dog, wagging his tail, a sign, I believe, that in those paltry beings corresponds to laughter and a smile, comes closer and curiously puts his wet nose to the uncorked flask; then, drawing back with sudden fear, barks at me as if reproaching me.


"Ah, miserable cur! If I had offered you a heap of excrement you would have sniffed it with delight, perhaps devouring it. Thus you, unworthy companion of my sad life, resemble the public, to whom one must never offer delicate perfumes that exasperate it, but carefully chosen garbage."
editorial_note: The translation preserves Baudelaire's prose satire: the dog rejects perfume just as the public rejects delicate art.

title: Art
text:
When the

spirit

fades

form

appears.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the stark lineation and aphoristic compression of the source.

title: Dog
text:
a single dog

walking alone on a hot

summer

sidewalk

seems to have the power

of ten thousand gods


why is that?
editorial_note: The translation preserves Bukowski's plain observation and final unadorned question.

title: Cause and Effect
text:
The best often die by

their own hand

just to escape,

and those left behind

can never understand

why anyone

would want

to escape

from

them.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the short descending line breaks and the bitter final turn toward those left behind.

title: There Are Worse Things Than...
text:
there are worse things than

being alone

but it often takes decades

to realize it

and more often

when this happens

it is too late

and there is nothing worse

than

a too late
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's conversational bluntness and the final noun-like 'too late.'
